overview: Auckland International Airport owns and operates New Zealand's largest and only true gateway international airport, sitting on 1,500 hectares on the Mangere peninsula and handling roughly 75% of the country's international arrivals and 66% of domestic seat capacity. The company runs a dual-till model combining Commerce Commission-monitored aeronautical charges (airfield and passenger services) with unregulated commercial operations spanning retail, car parking, and an increasingly large property and logistics portfolio. It also holds a 24.99% stake in Queenstown Airport, giving it exposure to New Zealand's key tourism gateway.

business_model.summary: Revenue is split roughly evenly between regulated/semi-regulated aeronautical income (airfield charges and passenger services charge, tied to passenger volumes and a Commerce Commission-overseen target return) and unregulated commercial income (retail concessions, car parking, and a growing rental/property book from logistics, office, retail and hotel assets). Aeronautical and retail revenue are largely transactional/volume-linked to passenger throughput; property rental income is long-duration, contracted and increasingly the more predictable growth engine as new developments are commissioned.

revenue_streams.name: Other (rates recoveries, interest income, other income)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (28 airlines, ~300 commercial tenants/retailers, logistics and office tenants) and B2C (~19m annual passengers, car park users, hotel guests)
business_model.geographic_mix: Single-site New Zealand asset (Auckland); revenue economically linked to international visitor arrivals (Australia, US, China as top source markets) and outbound Kiwi travel, plus domestic NZ property/logistics tenants

main_competitors: Sydney Airport (competing long-haul hub for transit/stopover traffic)
Alternative NZ logistics/industrial property landlords (Goodman Property Trust, Precinct Properties, Argosy)
competitive_position.market_position: De facto monopoly gateway for international air travel into New Zealand's largest city and economic hub; handles the majority of national international passenger and cargo volumes with very high barriers to a competing greenfield international airport

moat_factors.description: Only international airport serving Auckland (37%+ of NZ population); essentially impossible to replicate given land, consenting and capital requirements, giving durable market power that is nonetheless capped by Commerce Commission information-disclosure oversight rather than a free-market monopoly return
1,500ha landholding, single runway plus new domestic terminal and airfield expansion under construction; multi-decade asset life with high switching costs for airlines and tenants

658,000sqm of commercial property, logistics hub, hotels and a new outlet centre (Manawa Bay) generate contracted rental income (99% occupancy) that diversifies away from pure aeronautical/passenger cyclicality
Largest catchment and connectivity in NZ attracts airline capacity allocation over smaller regional airports, reinforcing hub status

weaknesses: Regulated aeronautical pricing is subject to Commerce Commission oversight (information disclosure regime) that constrains returns and creates political/airline pushback risk — the moat exists but the regulator, not AIA, effectively caps the ceiling on aeronautical returns
Heavily dependent on discretionary international/domestic travel demand and airline capacity decisions largely outside its control (e.g., Air New Zealand engine issues, global fuel price shocks)
Single-site concentration risk (seismic, volcanic, flooding — as experienced in the Jan-2023 floods) with no ability to diversify geographically

Currently running below the Commerce Commission's own target regulatory return (5.53% actual vs ~7.82% targeted for PSE4 to date), showing execution/timing risk in translating capex into allowed returns

growth_drivers: Multi-billion dollar terminal integration and domestic jet terminal programme (the domestic facility alone costed at ~$2.2bn, targeted completion ~2028-2029) adding 26% more domestic seat capacity and 44% more processing capacity
Airfield expansion (largest in company history, ~90% complete at H1-2026) adding resilience and six new remote aircraft stands
Property portfolio expansion - Manawa Bay outlet centre, Landing Business Park logistics developments (DHL Healthcare, IKEA), rent roll up 18% in FY25 with more pre-leased developments to come
New international air service connectivity (e.g., China Eastern's new Shanghai-Auckland-Buenos Aires route from Dec 2025) expanding transit and long-haul traffic
Recovery of international passenger volumes toward pre-COVID levels (92% of 2019 volumes as of FY25) as global aircraft fleet/engine constraints ease

Finalised 30-Jun-2026 Master Plan (first update in 10 years) targets ~38m passengers/year by the late 2040s (~2x current ~19m rolling 12-month volume), prioritising maximisation of existing infrastructure (efficiency/operational improvements) before committing to major new construction — a capital-discipline signal that should reduce the risk of another immediate capex supercycle once the current programme completes

Master Plan continues to safeguard land for a second (northern) runway ~2km from the existing one, but explicitly sets no build timeline pending further studies on demand, fleet mix and existing-runway efficiency — preserves long-run optionality without near-term capital commitment
Queenstown Airport equity stake (24.99%) provides indirect exposure to premium tourism catchment growth (Queenstown rolling 12-month passengers 2.82m)

business.description: Air New Zealand fleet/engine issues and Middle East conflict-driven fuel cost spikes have caused airlines (Air NZ, Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines) to cut capacity into/via Auckland; June 2026 traffic showed international seat capacity -2% and domestic capacity -6% YoY, driving passenger declines (international -4%, domestic -5%) even as underlying demand held up (load factors rose on some routes) and FY26 YTD total passengers remained +2%

Revenue is tied to discretionary travel; the June 2026 decline was capacity-driven rather than demand-driven (e.g., Middle East route passengers down 62% on a 53% capacity cut), but a sustained slower capacity recovery would still cap aeronautical/retail revenue growth
Seismic, volcanic and flood risk (2023 flood event still generating insurance recoveries/costs) with no geographic diversification

financial.description: FY26 capex guidance of $1.0-1.2 billion funded substantially by debt; NZ$1.31bn contractually committed at Dec-2025, total borrowings of ~$2.65bn, with execution/cost-overrun risk on the multi-year terminal and airfield programme; reported free cash flow deeply negative (~-NZ$570m in FY2025)
Significant bond, AMTN, bank facility and commercial paper borrowings; interest expense remains a meaningful drag on profit despite recent easing
Actual aeronautical return of 5.53% for PSE4-to-date versus a targeted 7.82%, meaning capex is not yet being fully recovered in earnings

regulatory.description: Aeronautical charges set under a five-year Price Setting Event cycle (currently PSE4, FY23-FY27) subject to ComCom review; AIA discounted charges for the final two years of PSE4 following the March 2025 final report, capping upside; formal PSE5 (covering FY2028-FY2032) consultation with airlines on capital costs and prices began from around July 2026 and is due to be finalised by mid-2027 — the ~$2.2bn domestic terminal only completes within the PSE5 window, so how those costs and any price-smoothing (flagged by the Commission for PSE5/PSE6) are treated is a major unresolved swing factor for aeronautical revenue from FY2028

regulatory.risk: Commerce Commission information disclosure and input methodology consultation
regulatory.description: ComCom's January 2026 process and issues paper proposed additional rules requiring earlier, more granular disclosure of major capital investment proposals (any project exceeding 20% of an airport's prior-year regulated asset base) for Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch airports, alongside potential amendments to the cost-of-capital input methodologies; public submissions (including from Air New Zealand, Qantas and NZ Airports) closed 23-Jul-2026 and cross-submissions (AIA lodged its own on 6-Mar-2026 responding to the original paper) are due 10-Aug-2026; no decision reached yet, but the outcome could tighten scrutiny of AIA's capex programme and/or lower allowed returns

High Court dismissed the merits review appeal by Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch airports and NZ Airports Association against the Commerce Commission's revised WACC methodology; ComCom published a cost-of-capital determination for disclosure year 2027 (5-May-2026) applying the framework, with a risk regulatory settings become permanently less favourable

regulatory.risk: Potential legislative change to airport regulation
regulatory.description: MBIE reviewed airport regulation effectiveness in 2025 and has since indicated it is not pursuing legislative change, but political/airline lobbying (including IATA calls for regulatory reform) for tighter regulation could resurface

macro.description: 2026 Middle East conflict drove jet fuel prices sharply higher (from ~US$85-90/bbl to US$150-200/bbl), prompting airlines including Air New Zealand to raise fares and cut capacity; June 2026 traffic data confirms the effect is still flowing through, with Middle East route passengers down 62% YoY on a 53% capacity cut, and broader international/domestic capacity down 2%/6% respectively

macro.risk: NZ and global consumer/discretionary spending slowdown
macro.description: Subdued NZ domestic economy has kept domestic passenger and retail spend growth muted
As a highly leveraged, long-duration infrastructure asset, AIA's valuation and funding costs are sensitive to NZ and global interest rate movements

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and NZ air travel continues a gradual post-COVID recovery, but the recovery has been disrupted through H1 2026 by a geopolitically-driven fuel price shock and constrained global aircraft/engine supply, creating near-term capacity headwinds (June 2026: international pax -4%, domestic pax -5% YoY, both capacity-driven) even as underlying long-term demand for NZ tourism and trade connectivity remains intact and FY26 year-to-date total passengers are still up ~2%
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high for aeronautical/retail/carpark revenue (tied to passenger and airline capacity cycles); low-to-moderate for the property segment (long leases, high occupancy provide ballast)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - large regulated capital base and debt-funded, multi-year capex programme make both cost of funding and asset valuation sensitive to interest rate moves
key_input_costs: Construction/materials costs for the terminal and airfield capex programme
Jet fuel prices (indirect, via airline capacity decisions rather than AIA's own cost base)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results (year ended 30-Jun-2026) are scheduled for release on 20-Aug-2026, with a CEO (Carrie Hurihanganui) and CFO (Stewart Reynolds) analyst/media webcast at 11am NZT — NOT YET RELEASED as of this analysis (9-Aug-2026); this report and all guidance/financial figures below predate that release and should be re-checked against it

Share price NZ$8.76; consensus analyst rating mixed Buy/Hold (4 buy, 6 hold, 0 sell across 10 analysts) with average 12-month price target ~NZ$8.69 (range NZ$7.02-9.31), implying the stock trades roughly in line with consensus fair value

June 2026 and FY2026-to-date traffic update: June international passengers 722,000 (-4% YoY) and domestic passengers -5% YoY, driven by reduced seat capacity (international -2%, domestic -6%) rather than weaker underlying demand — load factors held up or improved on several routes; Middle East routes the single largest drag (passengers -62%, capacity -53%); rolling 12-month Auckland passengers 19.04m, Queenstown 2.82m; FY26 year-to-date total passengers still +2%

Formal PSE5 (FY2028-2032) consultation with airlines on capital costs and pricing began around July 2026; the ~$2.2bn domestic jet terminal will not complete and open until 2028/2029, so its costs fall into the PSE5 window rather than PSE4 — a central input to this consultation, alongside the Commission's flagged interest in price-smoothing methods across PSE5/PSE6

Finalised 2025/26 Master Plan released (first comprehensive update in 10 years): targets ~38m passengers/year by the late 2040s (~2x current ~19m), prioritises maximising existing infrastructure and operational efficiency ahead of major new construction, continues to safeguard land for a second (northern) runway with no build timeline set pending further demand/fleet-mix studies, plus domestic/international terminal integration, cargo consolidation and climate resilience planning — read as a capital-discipline signal following the current capex supercycle

Commerce Commission consultation on changes to Airport Information Disclosure 2026 requirements: 20-Jan-2026 process and issues paper proposed additional rules for earlier/more granular disclosure of major airport capital investment proposals exceeding 20% of regulated asset base (Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch), alongside potential amendments to airport cost-of-capital input methodologies; AIA lodged a cross-submission (6-Mar-2026); public submissions from airlines/industry closed 23-Jul-2026 with cross-submissions due 10-Aug-2026 and no decision reached as of this update

Commerce Commission published its cost-of-capital determination for disclosure year 2027 for Auckland and Christchurch airports, applying the WACC methodology upheld by the High Court's dismissal of the airports' merits review appeal

H1 FY2026 interim results: revenue +4% to NZ$519.6m, EBITDAFI +6% to NZ$371.3m, net underlying profit +6% to NZ$157.1m, reported profit -5% to NZ$177.0m (lower investment property revaluation gain than pcp: $26.3m vs $50.5m), diluted EPS 10.38cps (vs 12.04cps pcp); passengers +2% to 9.64m; interim dividend 6.50cps
FY26 underlying profit guidance narrowed to $295-320 million (from $280-320 million at FY25 results) with capex guidance narrowed to $1.0-1.2 billion

Middle East conflict (from ~28 Feb 2026) drove jet fuel prices from ~US$85-90/bbl to US$150-200/bbl; Air New Zealand and other carriers (Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines) raised fares and cut long-haul capacity, a direct headwind to AIA passenger volumes into FY26/27, subsequently confirmed in the June 2026 traffic data; consensus analyst price target cut from NZ$9.00 to NZ$8.25 by RBC Capital (downgraded to Underperform from Outperform) on this uncertainty earlier in the year, with the broader average target since settling around NZ$8.69
China Eastern Airlines launched a new Shanghai-Auckland-Buenos Aires service via AKL (Dec-2025), estimated to deliver ~$110m in annual economic benefit to New Zealand

Auckland Council/Auckland Future Fund completed sale of its remaining ~9.71% stake in Auckland Airport for at least $8.08/share (~$1.31bn), ending decades of council ownership, following a 2023 partial sale of 7% at $8.11/share — AIA now has no single dominant council/government shareholder

Commerce Commission's final PSE4 report confirmed AIA's infrastructure investment programme as reasonable; AIA responded by discounting airline charges for the final two years of PSE4, targeting a 7.82% return (down from an earlier higher target) but reporting only 5.53% actual return to date

FY2025 annual results: revenue +12% to $1,004.7m, EBITDAFI +14% to $701.1m, underlying profit +12% to $310.4m, reported profit +7,549% to $420.7m (prior year had a one-off tax charge); total dividend 13.25cps (71.9% payout of underlying profit)

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Interim Results (19 February 2026); FY2026 annual results due 20 August 2026 (not yet released)

items.notes: Narrowed from the $280-320 million range given at FY25 results (Aug 2025); reflects continued passenger recovery and network growth momentum, but issued before the Middle East fuel-price shock reached its peak; no update to this range has been issued since 19-Feb-2026 as of this analysis — FY2026 annual results (20-Aug-2026) will show whether the June 2026 capacity-driven passenger declines pushed the outcome toward the lower end

items.vs_prior: narrowed from $1,000-1,300 million range given at FY25 results
items.notes: Focused on the domestic jet terminal (~$2.2bn total project cost, targeted completion 2028-2029), airfield expansion and commercial/property developments; NZ$1.31bn contractually committed at Dec-2025 across the multi-year programme

items.vs_prior: initial FY26 guidance given at FY25 results (Aug 2025)
items.notes: Given before the 2026 Middle East conflict/fuel spike and associated airline capacity cuts; June 2026 monthly data (international -4%, domestic -5% YoY) confirms actual outcomes are being pressured versus this base case, though FY26 year-to-date total passengers remained +2% as of the June update

items.target: 70-90% of underlying net profit after tax
items.notes: Dividend reinvestment plan (DRP) offered at a 2.5% discount; H1 FY26 interim dividend declared at 6.50 cents per share, fully imputed

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Carrie Hurihanganui highlighted continued network growth (e.g., new China Eastern service) and infrastructure delivery progress at the February 2026 interim result, while flagging that ongoing airline seat capacity constraints, the geopolitical environment, and a live construction environment create uncertainty around the FY26 outlook. The subsequent Middle East conflict and fuel price spike, and the confirmed capacity-driven passenger declines in the June 2026 traffic update, represent a live risk to the FY26 passenger and earnings guidance issued in February 2026; management has not issued a formal guidance update ahead of the 20-Aug-2026 FY2026 annual results release. Separately, the finalised Master Plan (30-Jun-2026) signals a more disciplined, staged approach to future capital investment beyond the current programme, deferring any second-runway decision. Formal PSE5 (FY2028-32) aeronautical pricing consultation with airlines began around July 2026 and is targeted for finalisation by mid-2027, with the ~$2.2bn domestic terminal's costs falling within that pricing window.

bull_case: Irreplaceable monopoly infrastructure asset serving New Zealand's largest city, with structural long-term growth underpinned by the newly finalised Master Plan targeting ~38m passengers/year by the late 2040s (~2x current volumes)
Diversified, high-occupancy (99%) property and logistics portfolio provides a growing, more predictable earnings stream that partially offsets aeronautical cyclicality

Multi-billion dollar capex programme (domestic terminal, airfield expansion, ~90% complete on airfield at H1-2026) directly expands capacity and, once commissioned, should convert into higher regulated and commercial revenue as the asset base grows; the Master Plan's emphasis on maximising existing infrastructure before new construction reduces the risk of an immediate second capex supercycle

Commerce Commission's PSE4 final report validated the reasonableness of AIA's investment programme, and the High Court upheld the Commission's WACC framework, removing an overhang of methodological uncertainty even as a narrower information-disclosure consultation continues

Progressive, high-payout dividend policy (70-90% of underlying profit) with a DRP, appealing to income-focused NZX investors, alongside a strong A- credit rating supporting continued access to debt funding; broadened shareholder base since Auckland Council's full 2023-24 exit removed council concentration risk; as one of very few large, liquid, NZX-listed monopoly infrastructure assets, AIA benefits from a structural scarcity bid from index funds, KiwiSaver default funds and NZ institutional investors with limited domestic alternatives
bear_case: The market price (~NZ$8.76) sits well above component-build DCF intrinsic value estimates (documented at ~NZ$1.90 base case in the DCF model) — a gap far too large to be explained by modelling conservatism alone; it reflects a persistent scarcity/infrastructure premium (index inclusion, thin NZX free float of comparable assets, KiwiSaver and passive fund mandates that must own it) rather than fundamentals, meaning a DCF-driven investor is knowingly paying for optionality and scarcity, not underlying cash generation, and the multiple has no obvious anchor if that premium ever compresses

June 2026 traffic data confirms the 2026 Middle East conflict and fuel price spike are actively cutting airline capacity into/via Auckland (international -2%, domestic -6% seat capacity YoY; Middle East route passengers -62%), directly pressuring FY26 passenger volumes just as FY26 guidance (issued Feb-2026) is tested at the 20-Aug-2026 annual result

Actual aeronautical returns (5.53%) remain well below the Commerce Commission's own targeted return (7.82%) for PSE4 to date, showing the enormous capex programme is not yet translating into commensurate earnings, with execution and cost-overrun risk through to terminal completion (2028-2029), and formal PSE5 (FY2028-32) pricing consultation — now underway and targeted for finalisation by mid-2027 — is an unresolved swing factor that could see the Commission push for further price smoothing or lower allowed returns on the ~$2.2bn domestic terminal spend

High leverage (~$2.65bn borrowings, NZ$1.31bn further committed capex) funding a multi-year capex programme leaves the company exposed to interest rate and refinancing risk, and to the risk that a live Commerce Commission consultation on tighter capex-disclosure rules and input methodologies (cross-submissions due 10-Aug-2026) further constrains allowed returns or delays project approvals

Consensus analyst price targets sit almost exactly at the current share price on average (~NZ$8.69 vs ~NZ$8.76), implying the market already prices in most known positives, with limited analyst-identified upside and a wide dispersion (NZ$7.02-9.31) reflecting genuine uncertainty linked to the Middle East conflict and capacity disruption continuing into FY2027

Single-site concentration risk (seismic, volcanic, flood) with no ability to diversify away from Auckland; the Master Plan's deferral of any second-runway decision, while capital-disciplined, also signals management does not see near-term capacity pressure requiring urgent expansion, potentially capping structural growth optionality
